title: Relocations, PIC and PIE
description: Choose the right relocation for a reference, explain what position independence actually costs, and recognise the two ways it goes wrong.
author: Underlayer
completion_criteria: Read all 9 concepts and reproduce the 61 measured checks in courses/reloc/assets/samples/crosscheck.py

concepts.title: One Relocation, or Two
concepts.description: The same source, two architectures, and a relocation count that follows from the instruction encoding.

concepts.title: Why There Are So Many Kinds
concepts.description: The x86-64 relocation set grouped by what it computes, and the encoding limits that created it.

concepts.title: The Limits That Shaped the Table
concepts.description: Reach, overflow and a zero displacement: the three encoding facts behind the vocabulary.

concepts.title: The Flags, and Which One Is Which Kind
concepts.description: -fPIC against -pie, and the binary that is neither because the two disagreed.

concepts.title: Does the Executable Actually Move?
concepts.description: Six runs, two builds, and the difference between a random base and a random address.

concepts.title: What Position Independence Costs
concepts.description: Nine instructions against seventeen, byte by byte, for the same eight additions.

concepts.title: The Relocation That Cannot Be Fixed
concepts.description: A failure class only PIC has, and a diagnostic that names both the type and the flag.

concepts.title: The One Relocation That Calls the Loader
concepts.description: Four thread-local models, and the one case where resolving a symbol means running code.

concepts.title: Applying Them Yourself
concepts.description: Read a real object file, apply its relocations at a chosen address, and run the result.

exercise_decls.question: Complete this sentence from the lesson: Read what that error is actually telling you. It does not say “wrong code” or “incompatible object”. It names the relocation type — ______ — and the symbol, and then it prescribes the flag. That specificity is the whole subject of this concept: a PIC violation is not a policy disagreement, it is a fact about a relocation type, and a fact can be named.
exercise_decls.explanation: The lesson states: Read what that error is actually telling you. It does not say “wrong code” or “incompatible object”. It names the relocation type — R_X86_64_32 — and the symbol, and then it prescribes the flag. That specificity is the whole subject of this concept: a PIC violation is not a policy disagreement, it is a fact about a relocation type, and a fact can be named.

exercise_decls.question: Complete this sentence from the lesson: That last line is the whole concept. There is no mechanism by which ______ can check what ld -no-pie will do, and no mechanism by which the linker can check what the compiler emitted. They are separate processes making a correlated decision, and the correlation is maintained by a build system.
exercise_decls.explanation: The lesson states: That last line is the whole concept. There is no mechanism by which clang -fPIE can check what ld -no-pie will do, and no mechanism by which the linker can check what the compiler emitted. They are separate processes making a correlated decision, and the correlation is maintained by a build system.
